subtitle: German in three countries: words, grammar and false friends
words.intro: You have learned German, and now you’ll go to Vienna and order an apricot and a coffee. They won’t understand you, or will pretend not to. There are three standard Germans, Germany’s, Austria’s and Switzerland’s, and none of them is the correct one.

grammar[0].fact: Swiss German writing has no *ß*: they write *Strasse* and *gross*. Austrians and southern Germans say *ich bin gesessen*, not *ich habe gesessen*. Neither of these is a mistake. Both are in the dictionary, marked with a small letter: A or CH.

grammar[1].blocks[0].title: Same word, other meaning
grammar[1].blocks[0].text: *der Sessel* in Austria is an ordinary chair. *der Estrich* in Switzerland is the attic.
grammar[1].blocks[1].title: How to say hello
grammar[1].blocks[1].note: *Grüß Gott* doesn’t mean you’re religious. *Moin* works at any hour.
grammar[1].blocks[2].text: Never tell an Austrian the *right* word. Say it their way, if you can, and if you can’t, smile. A German doing this is a Viennese comedy. A foreigner doing it may get an extra biscuit.
grammar[1].fact: German speakers have their own jokes about one another, and the old line says that Germans and Austrians are divided by their common language. In Swiss schools, children learn standard German almost as a foreign language. They speak dialect, write standard, and they’re very polite to visitors about all of it.

document.intro: A real old menu, from a restaurant in Vienna’s 7th district. Half of it is in French, which is how you knew it was good. Then look for the Viennese words: *Karfiol* (cauliflower), *Palatschinken* (pancakes), *Kaiserschmarrn* and *Schlagobers*.
document.fact: *Wiener Schnitzel* is a protected term in Austria: it has to be veal. Pork is *Schnitzel Wiener Art*. Do not get this wrong in front of Herr Franz.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Say what each one is in Germany.
reading.intro: Frau Huber is going to Vienna at last. It’s January. Inge has invited her, and Maya’s come along to carry the bag. They’re in a coffee house, the one where Karl stayed in 1978. Inge isn’t here yet. The waiter, Herr Franz, has worked here for 47 years, and he doesn’t care for Germans.
reading.photos[0].caption: Marillenknödel: Im Jänner sind sie aus dem Glas.
reading.fact: Austria has an official list of its own words that the EU had to accept: when it joined in 1995, a treaty protocol named 23 Austrian food words, including *Marillen*, *Erdäpfel* and *Paradeiser*. A Viennese waiter is a job of some standing, and the old titles like *Herr Doktor* are handed out with some generosity.
